newsitem.title: USA: Dole drives on despite scratchy voice on last day.
newsitem.headline: Dole drives on despite scratchy voice on last day.

text.p: Looking worn but still chipper, Bob Dole fought fatigue, a sandpaper-rough throat and voter apathy on Monday across the West, seeking an 11th hour surge for an epic victory over President Bill Clinton on Tuesday.
The odds were against the 73-year-old candidate winning on Tuesday as all polls showed him behind by about 8 to 13 percentage points but he kept on plugging.

His spirits were up despite campaigning with little sleep since Friday morning but the speeches that once lasted a half hour dwindled down to seven to 10 minutes, with him seemingly gagging out some crackled words from a raw throat.

But "the most optimistic man in America," as he likes to call himself, never showed signs of defeat as he steered his road show eastward from California with a hectic pace through eight states before he votes on Tuesday in his hometown of Russell, Kansas.
"I may not keep my voice but I will keep my word," Dole told about 3,000 cheering backers at a get-out-the-vote rally where former President George Bush introduced him as a man of integrity.
Aides said he was taking something called "throat coat" to soothe his weary voice from speech after speech at a pace of about one an hour.
Dole kept up his battering of Clinton over character and promised the Texans, "I will not violate the public trust when I'm president of the United States."
"I have never known such arrogance in the White House ... as I've witnessed on almost a daily basis in the Clinton White House."
"They say, 'well, we play by the rules.' They dont have any rules," said Dole. "They make up their own rules."

Dole started his last full day of campaigning before the election after midnight in Sacramento, California, and took his caravan to Phoenix; Alamogordo, New Mexico, and Houston, urging voters to go to the polls on Tuesday and seeking support from backers of Reform Party candidate Ross Perot.
Before voting in Russell, Dole will have touched down in Louisiana, Tennessee, Iowa and Missouri.

"I'm a little hoarse, but I'm in good shape," he told about 1,000 people in desolate Alamogordo, a scenic site ringed by mountains, home of the International Space Hall of Fame" and not far from where the first atomic bomb was tested in 1945.
Before dawn he spoke to a large crowd in Phoenix who waited for him for hours outside the "5 and Diner" -- a replica of a 1930s diner.
There he noted Sunday's Reuters/Zogby poll was a "dead heat" but in actuality it showed Clinton up by 3.8 points.
"If that poll is accurate and we're tied today, then we'll win tomorrow," Dole told the early morning throng.
The same poll on Monday showed Clinton moved up to a 7.3 percentage point lead, 44.2 percent to Dole's 36.9 percent with Perot 7 percent and over 10 percent undecided.

Aiming for a spectacular upset, Dole tells crowds, which are modest compared to Clinton's turnout, he is closing the campaign in the hometown of the late Democratic President Harry Truman, who won an historic upset over Thomas Dewey in 1948.
"I may be the Harry Truman of 1996," he told radio talk show host Don Imus on Monday.

The Dole campaign has travelled with an unusual assortment of celebrities that has included former Presidents Bush and Gerald Ford, sexy movie star Bo Derek, sugary singer Marie Osmond and Las Vegas headliner Wayne Newton.

On the final day of campaigning there were his buttoned- down staff members and his always properly attired wife Elizabeth offset by the bedraggled-looking Oak Ridge Boys, including one singer with gray hair down his back and beard to his chest.

In addition there is senior tour golfer Chi Chi Rodriguez -- with jet black, slicked down hair and glowing teeth -- who acts as a master of ceremonies introducing Dole and who advocates a constitutional amendment to bar "draft dodgers" from becoming president.

Representing the younger set is an eccentric-acting young conservative woman named only Kennedy, a star of the music cable network MTV, who urges young people to vote and who also makes a lot of faces at the crowds.
